| b. p-orbital | i. six electrons |

**a - iv.** Section 4.1.3 records that in 1932 James Chadwick identified the electrically neutral particle in the nucleus and "named this particle as **neutron**".

**b - i.** Section 4.7.2 gives \((2l + 1)\) orbitals for a subshell; for the p subshell \(l = 1\), so it has three orbitals. Section 4.7.5(ii) adds that an orbital holds at most two electrons with opposite spins. Hence a p subshell accommodates \(3 \times 2 = 6\) electrons.

**c - ii.** Table 4.1 lists the absolute charge on the electron as \(-1.6022 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}\).

**d - iii.** Table 4.5 places the Lyman series (\(n_1 = 1\)) in the Ultraviolet spectral region.

The name of each isotope carries its mass number \(A\). The atomic number \(Z\) is read off the periodic table, as the question's own hint directs. Then, by section 4.2, number of protons \(=\) number of electrons \(= Z\), and by \(N = A - Z\) the neutron count follows.

| Substance | Mass Number | Number of Protons | Number of Neutrons | Number of Electrons |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Carbon-14 | 14 | 6 | 8 | 6 |
| Lead-208 | 208 | 82 | 126 | 82 |
| Chlorine-35 | 35 | 17 | 18 | 17 |
| Uranium-238 | 238 | 92 | 146 | 92 |
| Oxygen-18 | 18 | 8 | 10 | 8 |
| Radium-223 | 223 | 88 | 135 | 88 |

The atomic numbers used are C 6, Pb 82, Cl 17, U 92, O 8 and Ra 88. Of these the chapter itself supplies only carbon (\(Z = 6\), Table 4.2), chlorine (\(Z = 17\), Problem 4.2) and oxygen (\(Z = 8\), Problem 4.12); lead, uranium and radium are not mentioned anywhere in this chapter and must come from the periodic table, which is what the printed hint is for.

Note that the electron count assumes a neutral atom — the question names substances, not ions, so \(Z\) electrons balance \(Z\) protons in every row.

By section 4.2, \(N = A - Z\), where \(A\) is the upper (left superscript) index and \(Z\) the lower (left subscript) index of each nuclide.

| Element | \(A\) | \(Z\) | \(N = A - Z\) | pairs with |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| a. \(^{40}_{18}\mathrm{Ar}\) | 40 | 18 | 22 | iv. 22 |
| b. \(^{14}_{6}\mathrm{C}\) | 14 | 6 | 8 | iii. 8 |
| c. \(^{40}_{19}\mathrm{K}\) | 40 | 19 | 21 | ii. 21 |
| d. \(^{14}_{7}\mathrm{N}\) | 14 | 7 | 7 | i. 7 |

So the matching is **a - iv, b - iii, c - ii, d - i**, and every entry in the second column is used exactly once.

The first two agree with worked results already in the chapter: Problem 4.1 computes 22 neutrons for \(^{40}_{18}\mathrm{Ar}\), and Table 4.2 lists 8 neutrons for \(^{14}_{6}\mathrm{C}\).

Section 4.2 gives \(A = Z + N\), so \(Z = A - N = 11 - 6 = 5\).

The same section states that an atom is represented "by element symbol (X) with the atomic mass number (\(A\)) as superscript on left and atomic number (\(Z\)) as subscript on left". Hence the representation is

\(^{11}_{5}\mathrm{X}\)
Hydrogen — section 4.5.2 states it in exactly these words: "Of all the elements, hydrogen has the simplest emission spectrum."

Section 4.6.5 states the principle as Heisenberg gave it in 1927: "**It is impossible to determine simultaneously, the exact position and exact momentum (or velocity) of an electron.**"

Mathematically it is expressed as \(\Delta x \times \Delta p_x \geq \dfrac{h}{4\pi}\), where \(\Delta x\) is the uncertainty in position and \(\Delta p_x\) the uncertainty in momentum — so the more precisely one is known, the less precisely the other can be.

There are four, listed in sections 4.7.1 and 4.7.2:

1. Principal quantum number, \(n\)
2. Azimuthal quantum number, \(l\) (also called the subsidiary quantum number)
3. Magnetic orbital quantum number, \(m_l\)
4. Electron spin quantum number, \(m_s\)

The first three come out of the solution of the Schrodinger equation and designate an orbital; the fourth was proposed by Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit (1925) and belongs to the electron, so "each electron [is] being assigned with four quantum numbers".

[Textbook misprint: the second group is printed as \(\mathrm{Ar}\), \(\mathrm{Cl^{2-}}\), \(\mathrm{K^{\oplus}}\). Chlorine (\(Z = 17\)) forms the UNInegative chloride ion \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\); a dinegative \(\mathrm{Cl^{2-}}\) would carry 19 electrons and so would NOT be isoelectronic with \(\mathrm{Ar}\) and \(\mathrm{K^{\oplus}}\), which both carry 18 — evidently what the group was set up to demonstrate, and what the chapter's own sentence on page 51 ("Species such as Ar, \(\mathrm{Ca^{2\oplus}}\) containing 18 electrons are isoelectronic with \(\mathrm{K^{\oplus}}\)") describes. The stem is transcribed exactly as printed and the solution below works out both readings.]

Section 4.7.6 defines isoelectronic species as "Atoms and ions having the **same number of electrons**". So count electrons in each species.

**First group.** \(\mathrm{Ne}\) has \(Z = 10\), so 10 electrons. \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\) is oxygen (\(Z = 8\)) with two electrons added: \(8 + 2 = 10\). \(\mathrm{Na^{+}}\) is sodium (\(Z = 11\)) with one electron removed: \(11 - 1 = 10\). All three have 10 electrons, so **\(\mathrm{Ne}\), \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\) and \(\mathrm{Na^{+}}\) are isoelectronic**, each with the configuration \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6\). Problem 4.12 works this same trio out.

**Second group, as printed.** \(\mathrm{Ar}\) has \(Z = 18\), so 18 electrons. \(\mathrm{K^{\oplus}}\) is \(19 - 1 = 18\) electrons, which the chapter states outright. But \(\mathrm{Cl^{2-}}\) would be \(17 + 2 = 19\) electrons, so as printed the three are not isoelectronic — only \(\mathrm{Ar}\) and \(\mathrm{K^{\oplus}}\) are.

**Second group with \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\).** \(17 + 1 = 18\) electrons, and then all three carry 18 electrons and the configuration \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6\) — matching the chapter's own sentence that "Species such as Ar, \(\mathrm{Ca^{2\oplus}}\) containing 18 electrons are isoelectronic with \(\mathrm{K^{\oplus}}\)".

| | Isotopes | Isobars |
|---|---|---|
| Definition | Atoms of the **same** element having the same number of protons but **different** numbers of neutrons in their nuclei | Atoms of **different** elements having the **same mass number** but different atomic numbers |
| Atomic number \(Z\) | Same | Different |
| Mass number \(A\) | Different | Same |
| Chemical identity | Same element | Different elements |
| Chemical properties | Similar | Different |
| Position in the modern periodic table | Same position | Different positions |
| Example | \(^{12}_{6}\mathrm{C}\), \(^{13}_{6}\mathrm{C}\), \(^{14}_{6}\mathrm{C}\) (Table 4.2) | \(^{14}_{6}\mathrm{C}\) and \(^{14}_{7}\mathrm{N}\) (Table 4.3) |

The two definitions are those of section 4.3(i) and 4.3(ii). The chapter adds that because the proton number is the atomic number, "all the isotopes of an element have the same position in the modern periodic table and exhibit similar chemical properties", whereas isobars "are different elements. They have different chemical properties and occupy different positions in modern periodic table."

**i. Isotones.** Section 4.3(iii): "The atoms of different elements having same number of neutrons in their nuclei are called isotones." Table 4.4 gives \(^{11}_{5}\mathrm{B}\) and \(^{12}_{6}\mathrm{C}\), each with \(N = 6\), as an example.

**ii. Isoelectronic species.** Section 4.7.6: "Atoms and ions having the same number of electrons are isoelectronic. The electronic configuration of the isoelectronic species is the same." For example \(\mathrm{K^{\oplus}}\), \(\mathrm{Ar}\) and \(\mathrm{Ca^{2\oplus}}\) all contain 18 electrons and share the configuration \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6\).

**iii. Electronic configuration.** Section 4.7.6: "Electronic configuration of an atom is the distribution of its electrons in orbitals." It is written by applying the aufbau principle, and may be shown either in orbital notation (\(n\mathrm{s}^a n\mathrm{p}^b n\mathrm{d}^c \ldots\)) or by the orbital diagram method.

**Statement.** Section 4.7.5(ii) gives Wolfgang Pauli's (1926) statement: "**No two electrons in an atom can have the same set of four quantum numbers.**" The chapter also gives the equivalent form: "**Only two electrons can occpy the same orbital and they must have opposite spins.**"

**Explanation.** An orbital is fully specified by the three quantum numbers \(n\), \(l\) and \(m_l\). Two electrons occupying the same orbital therefore already agree on all three, so the only quantum number left that can distinguish them is the spin quantum number \(m_s\). Since \(m_s\) has just two allowed values, \(+1/2\) and \(-1/2\), an orbital can hold at most two electrons, and those two must have opposite spins. Such a pair is called an **electron pair**.

**Illustration (the chapter's own).** Helium, \(Z = 2\), has the configuration \(1s^2\) with both electrons in the 1s orbital. Their two sets of quantum numbers, from Table 4.10, are

| Electron | \(n\) | \(l\) | \(m_l\) | \(m_s\) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1st electron | 1 | 0 | 0 | \(+1/2\) |
| 2nd electron | 1 | 0 | 0 | \(-1/2\) |

The two sets agree in \((n, l, m_l)\) and differ in \(m_s\), so they are not identical — as the principle requires.

**Consequence.** Because an orbital holds only two electrons and a shell with principal quantum number \(n\) contains \(n^2\) orbitals, the capacity of that shell is \(2n^2\) electrons.

**Statement.** Section 4.7.5(iii): "**Pairing of electrons in the orbitals belonging to the same subshell does not occur unless each orbital belonging to that subshell has got one electron each.**"

The orbitals of one subshell are degenerate (equal in energy), so an electron entering the subshell prefers an empty orbital to one already occupied, avoiding the repulsion of sharing.

**Example (the chapter's own).** Consider four electrons filling the p subshell, which has three degenerate orbitals. The first three go singly into the three orbitals; only the fourth is forced to pair. So the arrangement is

\(\uparrow\downarrow\ \ \uparrow\ \ \uparrow\)

and **not**

\(\uparrow\downarrow\ \ \uparrow\downarrow\ \ \text{(empty)}\)

The chapter adds the reason this matters: "half-filled and fully filled set of degenerate orbitals has extra stability", which is also what makes chromium and copper adopt anomalous configurations.

Section 4.4 gives two drawbacks.

**1. The model predicts an unstable atom.** In Rutherford's model electrons revolve about the nucleus, and orbital motion is accelerated motion because the direction of the velocity changes continuously. By Maxwell's electromagnetic theory an accelerated charged particle must emit electromagnetic radiation. An electron in an orbit would therefore radiate away the energy associated with its motion, and "the orbit would, therefore, shrink continuously. **Thus, an electron orbiting about the nucleus would follow a spiral path to the nucleus.**" The model thus has an intrinsic instability of the atom, whereas real atoms are stable.

(The electrons cannot be made stationary instead, because the electrostatic attraction would pull them straight into the nucleus, collapsing the model into Thomson's.)

**2. The model says nothing about electron arrangement or energy.** The second serious drawback is that it "**does not describe the distribution of electrons** around the nucleus **and their energies**".

Both drawbacks were overcome in the Bohr atomic model.

Section 4.6.1 lists four postulates of Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom.

**1. Fixed circular orbits.** The electron in the hydrogen atom can move around the nucleus in one of many possible circular paths of fixed radius and energy. These paths are called orbits, stationary states or allowed energy states, and are arranged concentrically around the nucleus in an increasing order of energy.

**2. Stationary states do not radiate.** The energy of an electron in an orbit does not change with time. The electron moves from a lower stationary state to a higher one only if and when the required amount of energy is absorbed, and energy is emitted when it moves from a higher stationary state to a lower one. The energy change does not take place in a continuous manner.

**3. Bohr's frequency rule.** The frequency of the radiation absorbed or emitted when a transition occurs between two stationary states differing in energy by \(\Delta E\) is

\(\nu = \dfrac{\Delta E}{h} = \dfrac{E_2 - E_1}{h}\)

where \(E_1\) and \(E_2\) are the energies of the lower and higher allowed energy states respectively.

**4. Quantisation of angular momentum.** The angular momentum of an electron in a given stationary state is an integral multiple of \(h/2\pi\):

\(mvr = n \times \dfrac{h}{2\pi}\), where \(n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots\)

Only those orbits satisfying this condition are allowed, so only certain fixed orbits exist.

Section 4.6.4 lists four limitations of the Bohr model.

**1.** It failed to account for the finer details of the hydrogen atom spectrum observed in sophisticated spectroscopic experiments.

**2.** It was unable to explain the spectrum of atoms other than hydrogen. (The chapter notes elsewhere that Bohr's theory applies only to hydrogen and hydrogen-like species, which contain a single extranuclear electron.)

**3.** It could not explain the splitting of spectral lines in the presence of a magnetic field (the Zeeman effect) or of an electric field (the Stark effect).

**4.** It failed to explain the ability of atoms to form molecules by chemical bonds.

Section 4.6.5 adds the deeper reason the model had to be replaced: it treats the electron as a charged particle on a well-defined circular path, which assumes that the position and the momentum of the electron are both known exactly at the same time — and that is ruled out by the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. It also takes no account of de Broglie's dual behaviour of matter.

Section 4.7.5 states that in the ground state electrons are filled into the orbitals in increasing order of energy, and section 4.7.4 fixes that order by the \((n + l)\) rule: the lower the sum \((n + l)\), the lower the energy; and if two orbitals have the same \((n + l)\), the one with the lower \(n\) is filled first.

Applying the rule, the order of filling in multi-electron atoms is

\(1s < 2s < 2p < 3s < 3p < 4s < 3d < 4p < 5s < 4d < 5p < 6s < 4f < 5d < 6p < 7s \ldots\)

The two apparent inversions both follow from the rule rather than breaking it: 4s (\(n + l = 4 + 0 = 4\)) fills before 3d (\(3 + 2 = 5\)), and 4f (\(4 + 3 = 7\)) fills after 6s (\(6 + 0 = 6\)). Where the sums tie — 3p and 4s at 4, 3d and 4p at 5 — the smaller \(n\) wins, so 3p precedes 4s and 3d precedes 4p (Table 4.9).

Fig. 4.10 gives the usual memory device for this sequence: write the subshells in rows by shell and read along the diagonal arrows.

Aufbau is a German word meaning 'building up', and the principle rests on three things together (section 4.7.5): the increasing order of orbital energies, the Pauli exclusion principle and Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity.

Section 4.7.5(iii) notes that a **half-filled or fully filled set of degenerate orbitals has extra stability**. In chromium and copper that extra stability outweighs the small cost of promoting one 4s electron into 3d, so the observed configuration is not the one aufbau filling alone would predict.

**Chromium, \(Z = 24\).** The expected configuration is \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6 4s^2 3d^4\). Here 3d is not half-filled and the atom has less stability. Interelectronic repulsion makes one 4s electron enter one of the empty 3d orbitals, whereupon **both** 4s and 3d become half-filled, and chromium acquires extra stability. Its configuration is therefore

\(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6 4s^1 3d^5\), that is \([\mathrm{Ar}]4s^1 3d^5\)

**Copper, \(Z = 29\).** The expected configuration is \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6 4s^2 3d^9\). Here the 3d subshell is neither half-filled nor fully filled. Interelectronic repulsion forces one 4s electron into 3d, which makes 3d completely filled with 4s half-filled, and copper acquires extra stability. Its configuration is therefore

\(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6 4s^1 3d^{10}\), that is \([\mathrm{Ar}]4s^1 3d^{10}\)

Both values agree with Table 4.12, which lists \([\mathrm{Ar}]4s^1 3d^5\) for chromium and \([\mathrm{Ar}]4s^1 3d^{10}\) for copper.

[Textbook misprint: the stem prints "quantum numbrs" for quantum numbers. Note also that the azimuthal quantum number is set upright in this item rather than in the italic \(l\) the rest of the chapter uses, so on the printed page it is not typographically distinguishable from the digit 1; it is read here as \(l\), since "\(n = 2\), \(1 = 1\)" would name no quantity. Neither point affects the answer.]

In the orbital notation (section 4.7.6) a subshell is written as the principal quantum number followed by the letter symbol of the subshell, with the number of electrons as a superscript. Section 4.7.2 fixes the letter: \(l = 0, 1, 2, 3\) correspond to s, p, d, f respectively.

**a. \(n = 2\), \(l = 1\).** \(l = 1\) is the p subshell, so the subshell is **2p**. Being a p subshell it has \(2l + 1 = 3\) orbitals, holding up to 6 electrons; a full subshell is written \(2p^6\).

**b. \(n = 4\), \(l = 2\).** \(l = 2\) is the d subshell, so the subshell is **4d**, with \(2l + 1 = 5\) orbitals holding up to 10 electrons; written full, \(4d^{10}\).

**c. \(n = 3\), \(l = 2\).** Again \(l = 2\) is the d subshell, so the subshell is **3d**, with 5 orbitals holding up to 10 electrons; written full, \(3d^{10}\).

Each pair is a legitimate combination, since \(l\) must lie in the range 0 to \((n - 1)\): \(1 \leq 1\) for (a), \(2 \leq 3\) for (b) and \(2 \leq 2\) for (c).

**Fe, \(Z = 26\).** Filling 26 electrons by the aufbau order of section 4.7.4 gives, as Table 4.12 lists for iron,

\(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6 3d^6 4s^2\), that is \([\mathrm{Ar}]4s^2 3d^6\)

**\(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\).** A dipositive cation is the atom with two electrons removed, so it has \(26 - 2 = 24\) electrons. Electrons are lost from the outermost shell first — the shell of highest principal quantum number — which here is the \(n = 4\) shell, so both 4s electrons go:

\(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6 3d^6\), that is \([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^6\)

**\(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\).** Three electrons removed leaves \(26 - 3 = 23\) electrons: the two 4s electrons and then one 3d electron.

\(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6 3d^5\), that is \([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^5\)

Note that \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) ends with a **half-filled** 3d subshell, which by section 4.7.5(iii) carries extra stability — the same argument the chapter uses for chromium.

[Note: the chapter states the rule for forming a cation only through a single worked instance — "Consider \(\mathrm{K^{\oplus}}\) formed by removal of one electron from K atom", where the electron lost is the outermost 4s one. It does not state the general rule that for a transition metal the ns electrons are removed before the \((n-1)\)d electrons; that rule is used here because it is the only reading consistent with the chapter's own example.]

Section 4.7.6 explains the condensed notation: the electronic configuration of the **preceding inert gas** is written as its symbol in a square bracket (this is the core part), and the outer configuration specific to the element is written immediately after the bracket.

| Element | \(Z\) | Full orbital notation | Condensed notation |
|---|---|---|---|
| a. Lithium | 3 | \(1s^2 2s^1\) | \([\mathrm{He}]2s^1\) |
| b. Carbon | 6 | \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^2\) | \([\mathrm{He}]2s^2 2p^2\) |
| c. Oxygen | 8 | \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^4\) | \([\mathrm{He}]2s^2 2p^4\) |
| d. Silicon | 14 | \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^2\) | \([\mathrm{Ne}]3s^2 3p^2\) |
| e. Chlorine | 17 | \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^5\) | \([\mathrm{Ne}]3s^2 3p^5\) |
| f. Calcium | 20 | \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6 4s^2\) | \([\mathrm{Ar}]4s^2\) |

The inert-gas core used is the nearest one **below** the element: He (\(1s^2\), \(Z = 2\)) for lithium, carbon and oxygen; Ne (\(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6\), \(Z = 10\)) for silicon and chlorine; and Ar (\(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6\), \(Z = 18\)) for calcium. Every row agrees with Table 4.12.

The diagrams asked for are the boundary surface diagrams of section 4.7.3; the chapter's own Fig. 4.7(b) and Fig. 4.8 accompany this answer. A boundary surface is drawn where the probability density \(\psi^2\) is constant, enclosing a region within which the chance of finding the electron is typically more than 90%.

**2s orbital.** A single sphere centred on the nucleus. All s orbitals are spherical, and the sphere grows with \(n\), so the 2s sphere is larger than the 1s sphere. The 2s electron cloud carries one **node** — a region of nearly zero probability density where the wave function changes sign — which shows in the probability density plot of Fig. 4.7(a) as a pale ring inside the cloud.

**2p orbitals.** There are three of them, \(2p_x\), \(2p_y\) and \(2p_z\), because for \(l = 1\) there are \(2l + 1 = 3\) allowed values of \(m_l\). Each is **dumb-bell** shaped: two lobes lying on opposite sides of a nodal plane that passes through the nucleus, so the probability of finding the electron in that plane is very close to zero. The three are identical in size and energy and differ only in orientation — their lobes lie along the \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) axes respectively.

So the drawing is: one sphere labelled 2s, and three two-lobed dumb-bells labelled \(2p_x\), \(2p_y\) and \(2p_z\), drawn along the three mutually perpendicular axes with the nucleus at the origin.

The azimuthal quantum number \(l\), also called the subsidiary quantum number, is significant in the following ways (section 4.7.2).

**1. It identifies the subshell.** Atomic orbitals with the same \(n\) but different \(l\) constitute a subshell belonging to that shell. The values \(l = 0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots\) are represented by the symbols s, p, d, f respectively.

**2. Its range fixes how many subshells a shell has.** \(l\) runs from 0 to \((n - 1)\), so the number of subshells in a shell equals \(n\). Thus the K shell (\(n = 1\)) has only one subshell (\(l = 0\)), the second shell has two and the third shell has three.

**3. It fixes the number of orbitals in the subshell.** For a given \(l\) there are \((2l + 1)\) values of \(m_l\), so the subshell contains \((2l + 1)\) orbitals — 1 for s, 3 for p, 5 for d, 7 for f (Table 4.7).

**4. It determines the shape of the orbital.** \(l = 0\) gives the spherical s orbitals, \(l = 1\) the dumb-bell p orbitals, \(l = 2\) the d orbitals of Fig. 4.9, and so on.

**5. It contributes to the orbital energy in multi-electron atoms.** In hydrogen-like species the energy depends on \(n\) alone, but "in the case of multi-electron atoms the energy of orbital depends on two quantum numbers \(n\) and \(l\) as well" — through the \((n + l)\) rule of section 4.7.4.

Section 4.7.2 gives \(l\) the range 0 to \((n - 1)\). For \(n = 3\), therefore

\(l = 0,\ 1,\ 2\)

and the third shell contains three subshells, 3s, 3p and 3d.

The same section gives \((2l + 1)\) values of the magnetic quantum number for each \(l\), running \(m_l = -l, \ldots, 0, \ldots, +l\). Hence

| \(l\) | Subshell | \(m_l\) | Number of orbitals \(= 2l + 1\) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 3s | 0 | 1 |
| 1 | 3p | \(-1,\ 0,\ +1\) | 3 |
| 2 | 3d | \(-2,\ -1,\ 0,\ +1,\ +2\) | 5 |

The total number of orbitals in the shell is \(1 + 3 + 5 = 9\), which is the expected \(n^2 = 3^2 = 9\) of Table 4.7.

Because of **Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity** (section 4.7.5 iii): "Pairing of electrons in the orbitals belonging to the same subshell does not occur unless each orbital belonging to that subshell has got one electron each."

Oxygen has \(Z = 8\), so after \(1s^2 2s^2\) there are four electrons left for the 2p subshell. The three 2p orbitals \(2p_x\), \(2p_y\) and \(2p_z\) are **degenerate** — identical in size and energy, differing only in orientation — so the first three of those electrons occupy them singly, one each. Only the fourth electron is obliged to pair up, and it does so in the orbital that the filling order reaches first. That gives

\(1s^2\ 2s^2\ 2p_x^{\,2}\ 2p_y^{\,1}\ 2p_z^{\,1}\)

The rejected arrangement \(1s^2\ 2s^2\ 2p_x^{\,2}\ 2p_y^{\,2}\ 2p_z^{\,0}\) pairs the third and fourth electrons in \(2p_y\) while leaving \(2p_z\) completely empty, so it breaks the rule directly: pairing has begun before every orbital of the subshell holds one electron.

Physically, two electrons crowded into one orbital repel each other, so the arrangement with the electrons spread over separate orbitals is of lower energy and greater stability. The chapter makes the same point through its worked case of four electrons in a p subshell, where the correct filling is \(\uparrow\downarrow\ \uparrow\ \uparrow\) and not \(\uparrow\downarrow\ \uparrow\downarrow\) with the third orbital empty. Note that both configurations hold the same eight electrons — the two are not distinguished by electron count but by how the four 2p electrons are distributed.

**Principal quantum number, \(n\)** (section 4.7.2).

**Values.** \(n\) is a positive integer: \(n = 1, 2, 3, 4, \ldots\) It is one of the three quantum numbers that come out of the solution of the Schrodinger equation for the hydrogen atom, and in Bohr's model it is the number labelling the stationary states.

**What it identifies.** It identifies the **shell**. All atomic orbitals having the same value of \(n\) belong to the same shell, and the shells are denoted by the symbols K, L, M, N, ... for \(n = 1, 2, 3, 4\) respectively (Table 4.6).

**Number of orbitals.** The number of allowed orbitals in a shell increases with \(n\) and is \(n^2\) — 1 for the K shell, 4 for L, 9 for M and 16 for N. Since an orbital holds at most two electrons, the electron capacity of the shell is \(2n^2\).

**Number of subshells.** The shell with principal quantum number \(n\) contains exactly \(n\) subshells, because \(l\) runs from 0 to \((n - 1)\).

**Size and distance.** With an increase of \(n\), the distance from the nucleus and the size of the shell increase. The radius of a stationary state is \(r_n = n^2 a_0\) with \(a_0 = 52.9\) pm, so the Bohr radius 52.9 pm is the radius of the first state.

**Energy.** The energy also increases with \(n\), becoming lesser and lesser negative: \(E_n = -R_H\left(\dfrac{1}{n^2}\right)\) with \(R_H = 2.18 \times 10^{-18}\ \mathrm{J}\). The lowest energy state, \(n = 1\), is the **ground state**. In hydrogen-like species the orbital energy depends on \(n\) alone; in multi-electron atoms it depends on \(n\) and \(l\) together.

The M shell has principal quantum number \(n = 3\) (Table 4.6).

**Subshells.** \(l\) runs from 0 to \((n - 1)\), so \(l = 0, 1, 2\) and the M shell has three subshells: 3s, 3p and 3d.

**Orbitals.** Each subshell holds \((2l + 1)\) orbitals.

**Electrons.** Each orbital holds at most two electrons of opposite spin, by the Pauli exclusion principle.

| Subshell | \(l\) | Orbitals \(= 2l + 1\) | \(m_l\) values | Maximum electrons |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3s | 0 | 1 | 0 | 2 |
| 3p | 1 | 3 | \(-1,\ 0,\ +1\) | 6 |
| 3d | 2 | 5 | \(-2,\ -1,\ 0,\ +1,\ +2\) | 10 |
| **Total** | | **9** | | **18** |

So the M shell contains **9 orbitals** and can accommodate a maximum of **18 electrons**, distributed as \(3s^2\ 3p^6\ 3d^{10}\).

Both totals agree with the general results of the chapter: the number of orbitals in a shell is \(n^2 = 3^2 = 9\) (Table 4.7), and the capacity of a shell is \(2n^2 = 2 \times 9 = 18\) (section 4.7.5).

Write each configuration and then fill the outermost subshell by Hund's rule, which puts one electron into each degenerate orbital before any pairing begins.

**a. Silicon, \(Z = 14\).**

\(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^2\), that is \([\mathrm{Ne}]3s^2 3p^2\) (Table 4.12)

Every subshell up to 3s is completely filled, so all of those electrons are paired. The two 3p electrons occupy two different 3p orbitals with parallel spins, leaving the third 3p orbital empty:

3p: \(\uparrow\ \ \uparrow\ \ \text{(empty)}\)

**Silicon has 2 unpaired electrons.**

**b. Chromium, \(Z = 24\).**

Chromium is one of the two anomalous cases of section 4.7.5. Its configuration is not \([\mathrm{Ar}]4s^2 3d^4\) but

\(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6 4s^1 3d^5\), that is \([\mathrm{Ar}]4s^1 3d^5\) (Table 4.12)

The argon core is fully paired. The single 4s electron is unpaired, and the five 3d electrons occupy the five 3d orbitals singly, again by Hund's rule:

4s: \(\uparrow\)   3d: \(\uparrow\ \ \uparrow\ \ \uparrow\ \ \uparrow\ \ \uparrow\)

\(1 + 5 = 6\), so **chromium has 6 unpaired electrons**.

It is worth noting that the expected configuration \([\mathrm{Ar}]4s^2 3d^4\) would give only 4 unpaired electrons, so this answer depends on using the anomalous configuration the chapter states.

**a. Number of protons.** Section 4.2 states that an atom is electrically neutral, so it "contains the same number of extranuclear electrons in it as its atomic number", that is number of protons \(=\) number of electrons \(= Z\). With 29 electrons,

number of protons \(= Z = 29\)

(The mass number follows too, if wanted: \(A = Z + N = 29 + 35 = 64\).)

**b. Electronic configuration.** \(Z = 29\) is copper, one of the two anomalous cases of section 4.7.5. Filling by aufbau alone would give \([\mathrm{Ar}]4s^2 3d^9\), in which the 3d subshell is neither half-filled nor fully filled; interelectronic repulsion forces one 4s electron into 3d so that 3d becomes completely filled and 4s half-filled, which carries extra stability. Hence

\(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6 3d^{10} 4s^1\)

or in condensed notation \([\mathrm{Ar}]4s^1 3d^{10}\), exactly as Table 4.12 lists for copper.

As a check, the superscripts sum to \(2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 6 + 10 + 1 = 29\), matching the electron count given.
